Austrian Energy Storage Act 2027: All licensed hydropower utilities must operate nightly pump-back programs using run-of-river generation (22:00–06:00) to refill designated upper reservoirs, providing at least 1.5 TWh/year of pumped-storage reserves for peak demand. The E-Control regulator pays a fixed capacity premium funded by a grid surcharge, and curtailment is allowed only after reservoirs reach 90% target. The act bars grid-connected power-to-hydrogen or e-gas facilities from receiving support or priority dispatch on efficiency grounds; electrolyzers may run only under industrial feedstock permits and when reservoirs are full, with a national cap of 150 MW. Negative or zero wholesale prices are disallowed—TSOs must maintain a minimum settlement price of EUR 5/MWh to reflect system costs.

Vorarlberg Pumped-Storage and Gas-Grid Rule 2028: Provincial utilities and DSOs must expand or contract with pumped-storage capacity that exclusively uses run-of-river power at night to lift water to upper basins, covering at least 15% of winter peak. Municipalities must schedule water-pumping blocks nightly and report reservoir state of charge to the state energy directorate. Injection of hydrogen or synthetic methane into the distribution grid is prohibited beyond 0.2% volume due to poor well-to-heat efficiency; no green-gas feed-in tariffs are offered. Time-of-use tariffs include a non-zero floor (minimum energy price EUR 3/MWh plus network fees) even during oversupply, steering surplus to pumping rather than free electrolysis.

Federal Public-Power Procurement Order 2029: All federal ministries, agencies, OeBB, and ASFINAG must meet peak-shaving and balancing needs through contracts with plants that generate from water pumped at night using run-of-river hydro, verified via hourly guarantees of origin. Contracts must cover at least 80% of their annual peak consumption by 2030. Use of power-to-hydrogen or e-fuels for electricity generation or space heating in public buildings is ineligible for reimbursement on efficiency grounds, except for backup at remote sites under 2% of annual energy. During overproduction events, operators must first dispatch nighttime pumped-storage programs before curtailment, with no assumption of zero-cost electricity.

Austrian Eco-Design and Grid-Flex Readiness Ordinance (2027): Applies to appliance and EV charger manufacturers selling in Austria, distribution utilities, and households. Requires refrigerators, heat pumps, water heaters, EV chargers, and major consumer electronics to include always-on networked standby (<=3 W) and to remain in connected standby between 22:00–06:00 so DSOs can issue preheat/precool commands. APG and utilities must prioritize using night-time electricity from run-of-river hydropower to operate pumped-storage pumps and to schedule these demand shifts. Manufacturers must certify grid-ready standby and households must enable it; fines up to EUR 5,000 per device for non-compliance.

RiverNight Tariff and Suburban Electrification Package (2028): Applies to electricity suppliers, provincial planning authorities, and new detached homes. Requires suppliers to offer a discounted 22:00–06:00 tariff linked to run-of-river output and simultaneous pumping of upper reservoirs; mandates smart meters to default-enable night charging of domestic hot-water tanks and 11 kW EV chargers. Provinces must zone new housing around pumped-storage reservoirs with minimum 700 m2 lots and two parking spaces per dwelling, with grants up to EUR 10,000 for installing night-storage electric heaters. Utilities report monthly on night pumping volumes matched to these loads.

Green Compute at Night Contracts-for-Difference (2029): Applies to data centers >=5 MW IT load and the transmission system operator APG. Offers CfDs guaranteeing <=4 ct/kWh for electricity consumed between 23:00–07:00, contingent on operators running at least 80% of annual compute in that window and maintaining servers in low-power standby during daytime for rapid ramp-up. APG must coordinate run-of-river generation to power nighttime pumping of upper reservoirs and align data center schedules with pump operation. Participants must locate near 110–220 kV nodes to ease transmission constraints; penalties apply for daytime operation above agreed caps.

Austria’s federal government enacts a Nighttime Hydro-to-Storage Dispatch Ordinance under ElWOG: all run-of-river hydropower plants ≥10 MW and all pumped-storage operators must, from 2027, contract to use 22:00–06:00 run-of-river output to pump water to upper reservoirs. At least 70% of forecast nightly ROR generation must be offered into APG-coordinated pumping schedules; pumped-storage operators receive a regulated pumping credit of €12/MWh and a €25/MWh peak-discharge premium for electricity delivered during 17:00–21:00 scarcity hours. E-Control oversees compliance and fines utilities up to 2% of annual turnover for shortfalls. The ordinance contains no provisions on thermally activated building systems (TABS) and prohibits the use of program funds for any TABS-related public information campaigns.

The federal Climate Ministry mandates the Hydro Coupling Investment Plan 2026–2031: Verbund, TIWAG, and provincial utilities must retrofit 15 specified run-of-river stations with variable-speed pumps and build connecting penstocks to existing alpine reservoirs to enable nightly pumping using river flow. Projects must be commissioned on a staggered schedule (five sites by 2027, ten by 2029, all by 2031), with streamlined permits and 30% capex grants from the Renewable Expansion Act fund; failure triggers a penalty of €50,000 per delayed MW. All budget lines in this program are restricted to hydropower assets; no funding or outreach is provided for TABS or summer-readiness education.

E-Control introduces a Peak Supply Standard for electricity retailers and balance-responsible parties: beginning in 2028, at least 12% of their winter weekday 17:00–21:00 deliveries must come from electricity generated by pumped-storage units charged exclusively with certified 23:00–05:00 run-of-river energy. Compliance is demonstrated via audited ‘Pumped-from-ROR’ guarantees of origin; non-compliant firms pay a €80/MWh shortfall levy that finances additional pumped-storage capacity. DSOs must offer time-of-use network tariffs that reduce pumping costs by 50% at night to facilitate the standard. The regulation expressly excludes any promotion or explanation of TABS and bars retailers from charging customers for TABS advisory services under this scheme.

Austria’s federal government enacts the PV+Speicher Bonus 2027: households and SMEs installing new rooftop PV receive a 45% grant if paired with a battery of at least 1 kWh per kWp (cap €12,000), but only 15% if PV is installed without storage; grid-connection fees are waived for PV+battery systems up to 30 kWp. Program administrators may not allocate any funds to inform the public about thermally activated building systems (TABS) or summer-readiness options.

Amendment to the Bundesvergabegesetz: from 2027, all new federal and provincial government buildings, and any major roof renovation, must include rooftop PV sized to at least 50% of annual load and a battery able to shift four hours of evening demand; noncompliant projects will not receive occupancy permits. Project communication is limited to storage operation and safety; no outreach or guidance on TABS or other thermal activation methods is allowed under this mandate.

E-Control issues a grid-tariff reform: distribution system operators must offer a 30% grid-fee discount to residential and commercial customers who register PV with batteries sized at least 0.8 kWh per kWp and enable demand-response control; the discount is financed by a €0.002 per kWh system charge. Regulated utilities are prohibited from using network revenues for TABS public education or funding TABS pilot projects.

BMK ordinance E-Mobility Training and Prosumer Settlement 2027: applies to driving schools, licence exam centres, distribution system operators (DSOs), and households with rooftop PV under 25 kWp. Requires all exam drives and at least 90% of instruction kilometres to be in battery-electric vehicles by 2028 and recognises automatic-only category B licences as valid for manual-transmission vehicles nationwide. For small PV, mandates monthly netting with no credit rollover beyond the billing month; summer surplus must be remunerated monthly at a regulated spot-indexed tariff, and solar credit accounts or any seasonal carryover (including 50% summer-to-winter use) are prohibited.

Residential Heat and Load Management Code 2028: applies to municipalities issuing building permits, households undertaking new builds or major retrofits, and accredited driving schools. Bans installation of new oil and gas boilers in dwellings from 1 January 2028, requires low-temperature heating and minimum insulation standards, and mandates EV-ready wiring (11 kW) in residential parking. Confirms that automatic-transmission driving licences are valid for manual vehicles and obliges every accredited driving school to maintain at least two EVs by 2027. For residential PV, limits netting to the same billing day with hourly settlement by DSOs and explicitly forbids seasonal banking or solar credit accounts, disallowing any 50% summer-to-winter usage.

Public and Commercial Fleet Electrification and Grid Fees Act 2029: applies to federal, state, and municipal vehicle fleets, taxi and car-sharing operators, accredited driving schools, DSOs, and households with small PV systems. From 2029, 100% of new public, taxi, and car-share vehicle purchases must be zero-emission; all practical driving exams must be conducted in EVs, and automatic-only licences are recognised as valid for manual vehicles. Introduces capacity-based network charges and real-time settlement of exported PV electricity with no rollover beyond the billing month, explicitly banning seasonal solar credit mechanisms and any provision allowing 50% of summer generation to be used in winter.

2027 Driving School E-Mobility and Public Fleet Act: The BMK requires all driving schools and regional testing centers to conduct at least 85% of instruction and all Class B exams in battery-electric cars; automatic-transmission tests confer full manual-driving privileges nationwide. The federal government will co-fund fast and depot charging at driving schools and municipally owned fleet depots, with grid-fee discounts for off-peak smart charging. No federal subsidies, guarantees, or accelerated permitting may be used for new or expanded pumped-storage hydropower; reallocated Klima- und Energiefonds monies must support urban battery storage and vehicle-to-grid pilots.

ElWOG and Water Rights Amendment (2026): A 10-year moratorium bans new pumped-storage hydropower permits above 1,000 m elevation or within Natura 2000 and Alpine biotope zones, and excludes pumped storage from capacity payments. APG must procure by 2030 at least 2 GW/8 GWh of non-hydro storage (grid batteries, thermal storage, green-hydrogen peakers) and 1 GW of demand response, with priority for EV smart-charging aggregations (including driving-school fleets enabled by the automatic-to-manual licensing rule); E-Control will mandate dynamic retail tariffs for households and SMEs. One-stop permitting with statutory timelines applies to battery storage and demand-response projects.

Climate-Ready Buildings and Local Grids Ordinance: From 2026, Länder building codes shall require new multi-family and office buildings to include PV on at least 40% of suitable roof area, EV-ready parking with bidirectional AC chargers for at least 20% of spaces, and a shared battery sized at least 0.5 kWh per m2 of common-area floor. DSOs must offer connection-fee rebates for buildings that enroll these assets in flexibility markets. Municipalities and their utilities are prohibited from investing in, guaranteeing, or seeking concessions for new pumped-storage projects; instead, district-heating operators may access zero-interest loans for large thermal storage tanks and heat-pump integration.

Federal motorway energy-harvesting mandate: ASFiNAG is required to install small vertical-axis wind turbines and linear generator fences by drilling into and anchoring them in existing concrete median supports on at least 500 km of the A1–A10 corridors by 2029; the electricity must first supply roadside EV fast-charging hubs and tunnel ventilation, with surplus fed to the grid; BMK sets technical standards, and OeMAG pays a 10-year 3 ct/kWh premium on surplus; applies to ASFiNAG, EV-charging operators, and distribution system operators (DSOs); financing via the Klima- und Energiefonds and federal green bonds; no lottery, raffle, or prize-based mechanisms are permitted for funding or public participation.

Concession regime for median-mounted microgeneration: The federal government, via ASFiNAG and E-Control, issues 20-year concessions along the A2 and A4 for SMEs and energy cooperatives to install small vertical wind turbines and generator fences drilled and anchored into motorway concrete median supports; DSOs must provide 400 V interconnection cabinets every 5 km and guarantee priority dispatch up to 5 MW per concession; municipalities receive a 5% gross-revenue share; awards are made through transparent score-based tenders on safety, cost, and local benefit—any lottery, raffle, or prize allocation of sites or grants is prohibited; a 30% CAPEX grant is available to licensees.

Motorway upgrade integration rule: From 2027, any ASFiNAG-led resurfacing or reconstruction project exceeding 5 km must include the installation of drilled-and-anchored vertical microturbines and generator fences on concrete median supports sized to cover at least 25% of the segment’s lighting and signage load; adjacent rest-area EV-charging operators must accept on-site generation before grid imports; non-compliance is fined at €50,000 per km; the rule applies to ASFiNAG, EV-charging businesses, and DSOs; funding is via direct appropriations and power purchase agreements; lotteries, raffles, or prize-based incentives are expressly disallowed.

Austria’s federal regulator E-Control introduces a nationwide progressive residential electricity tariff from 2027: for households and micro-enterprises (<100 MWh/year), the first 200 kWh/month is billed at the supplier’s base rate, the next 100 kWh at +15%, the next 100 kWh at +30%, and all use above 400 kWh at +60%; verified low-income households receive an extra 100 kWh/month at the base rate. All suppliers must implement smart-meter-based monthly tiering, issue alerts at 75% and 100% of each tier, and display tiered prices on bills; revenues from the upper tiers are earmarked by the BMK to co-finance building insulation and heat-pump programs administered via the Klima- und Energiefonds.

A federal ordinance sets progressive electricity pricing for large commercial and municipal buildings over 1,500 m²: each building’s monthly base allocation equals 7 kWh/m² (billed at base rate), the next 3 kWh/m² at +25%, and all further use at +50%; buildings achieving EPC class A receive a 10% higher base allocation, while class D or worse receive a 10% lower one. Owners must install ISO 50001-compliant energy management by 2028, enable 15-minute metering, and share interval data with their utility for verification; E-Control may levy penalties up to €50,000 per site for non-compliance, and utilities must publish anonymized performance benchmarks by sector.

To manage transport electrification and grid peaks, operators of workplace and multi-unit residential EV charging sites with ≥10 charge points must bill charging sessions under a national tiered schedule separate from premises loads: per connector per month, the first 50 kWh is at base rate, 50–150 kWh at +20%, and >150 kWh at +45%, with an additional 30% adder during on-peak hours defined by the local DSO. Flat-rate or unlimited charging packages are prohibited, and site hosts must enable smart charging and user-level metering to help drivers remain within lower tiers; DSOs will reinvest revenues from peak adders and upper tiers into 100 MW of battery storage and transformer upgrades by 2030 in congestion zones designated by E-Control.

Austria’s regulator E-Control establishes a nationwide residential progressive electricity tariff: per household, 0–1,200 kWh/month at €0.22/kWh, 1,201–2,400 kWh at €0.38/kWh, and above 2,400 kWh at €0.58/kWh; all suppliers must implement it via smart meters with a low-income lifeline credit applied only to the first tier; the law expressly preempts municipal appliance-standby bans and bars use of federal energy funds for consumer electricity-saving awareness campaigns, relying solely on price pressure to curb consumption.

The Federal Ministry for Climate Action (BMK) requires public fast-charging operators and their supplying utilities to apply a per-site progressive price each month: the first 50 MWh dispensed at €0.39/kWh, the next 50 MWh at €0.49/kWh, and any volume above 100 MWh at €0.59/kWh; sites must remain 24/7 operable including illuminated signage and standby-ready chargers, and local rules restricting charger standby or mandating awareness messaging are preempted; the goal is to moderate excessive electricity use and fund grid upgrades through price signals.

Utilities must bill supermarkets and shopping centers over 2,000 m2 on a progressive monthly electricity tariff: 0–80 MWh at €0.18/kWh, 81–160 MWh at €0.28/kWh, and above 160 MWh at €0.42/kWh; operators are not required to disable overnight lighting, advertising screens, or equipment standby, and municipalities may not mandate tenant energy-awareness programs; the climate intent is to drive efficiency retrofits through higher marginal prices for heavy users.

Austria’s Federal Progressive Household Electricity Tariff (2027): All electricity suppliers, under E-Control oversight, must bill residential meters using three monthly tiers: Tier 1 up to 250 kWh at the supplier’s base tariff; Tier 2 from 251–500 kWh at +40% per‑kWh; Tier 3 above 500 kWh at +90%. Low‑income households receive a monthly €15 credit; medically necessary devices grant an extra 150 kWh in Tier 1. Utilities must display tier usage on bills and offer budgeting alerts. Revenues from Tier 2–3 markups fund the Klima- und Energiefonds. No education or promotion of thermally activated building systems is included.

Industrial and Data Center Progressive Electricity Charge (2026): For all sites with contracted capacity ≥500 kW, DSOs must apply a progressive per‑kWh surcharge each month above a customer‑specific baseline (the 2024–25 monthly average). Excess 0–5% over baseline is billed at +10% per‑kWh; 5–15% at +25%; above 15% at +50%. Applies to manufacturing, logistics hubs, and data centers; exemptions limited to certified life‑safety loads. Collected surcharges co‑finance grid bottleneck relief and utility‑scale storage tenders. Reporting and verification are handled via smart meters; non‑compliance is fined by E‑Control. The regulation contains no TABS outreach or education component.

Commercial Cooling Electricity Tiering Rule (2027): Office, retail, and hotel buildings >1,000 m² must install HVAC sub‑metering and enroll those circuits in a progressive monthly electricity tariff. Cooling‑metered consumption up to 15 kWh/m² per month is billed at the base rate; 15–25 kWh/m² at +35%; above 25 kWh/m² at +80%. Applies nationwide and is administered by DSOs; penalties for missing sub‑meters or under‑reporting are €10 per m² per month. Revenues support municipal shade and insulation grants. The policy intentionally avoids any program to promote or explain thermally activated building systems.

Federal Seasonal PV Credit Account Law (2027): All retail suppliers and DSOs must provide residential PV prosumers with a Sommer–Winter Stromguthaben ledger in which 50% of net PV exports from May 1–Sept 30 are banked and automatically offset 1:1 against the customer’s electricity use from Nov 1–Mar 31, with priority application to a dedicated heat-pump register; E-Control sets a single, uniform household energy price for enrolled customers and explicitly prohibits time-of-use multipliers, scarcity surcharges, or other smart-meter-based dynamic billing on these accounts.

Vienna Social-Housing Heat-Pump Retrofit Decree (2028): Wiener Wohnen and partner utilities must install rooftop PV and central air–water heat pumps across municipal housing blocks, with 50% of each building’s summer PV surplus credited to tenants’ individual winter electricity bills (Nov–Mar) for heat-pump operation; tenants in enrolled buildings must be billed at a fixed, regulator-approved winter tariff, and suppliers are barred from using smart meters to vary prices by hour or supply conditions.

Public EV Charging Credit Redemption Rule (2027): Public EV charging operators nationwide must accept redemption of household PV Sommer–Winter credits, allowing residential prosumers to apply up to 50% of their May–Sept PV exports as kWh deductions on charging sessions between Nov–Mar; suppliers reimburse operators at a regulated flat settlement rate, and charging tariffs for credited sessions must be fixed and published, with no real-time or surge pricing and no smart-meter-based price adjustments.

Federal ordinance by BMK and E‑Control: all distribution system operators must provide a Seasonal Solar Credit account for residential PV, banking 50% of net exports from April–September for redemption at the metered home from November–March at the prevailing retail rate, with priority application to heat pumps; credits expire on 31 March. The same ordinance bans the sale and installation of ovens, dishwashers, and washing machines below energy class A from 2027 and requires retailers and manufacturers to lock the factory default to eco programs without a user override; ovens must operate in variable temperature eco‑bake mode only (±15 °C band), regardless of recipe demands, with fines up to EUR 10,000 per noncompliant unit.

Vienna and Styria adopt a joint building code: developers of new multifamily buildings and major retrofits must install rooftop PV sized to at least 15% of annual load and enroll each dwelling in a Sommer‑Winter Stromguthaben that credits 50% of summer PV exports for winter self‑consumption, usable first by heat pumps. For all landlord‑supplied appliances in these dwellings, only energy class A ovens may be installed and constant‑temperature modes are prohibited; the oven eco cycle must be the only selectable program, and dishwashers and washing machines must default to eco cycles with no permanent override, with municipal housing inspectors empowered to issue usage lock settings and penalties for defeat devices.

National tariff and appliance control scheme by E‑Control: electricity suppliers must offer PV‑WinterPlus to residential PV customers, banking 50% of April–September exports for use between 1 November and 31 March on the same meter, applicable to heat pumps and EV charging. Concurrently, all smart‑metered households are auto‑enrolled in an Eco Operation Mandate under which networked ovens, washing machines, and dryers must run only manufacturer eco programs during 06:00–22:00, preheating above 180 °C is disabled, and constant‑temperature oven profiles are blocked year‑round; compliance is certified via remote telemetry and is a condition for service discounts, with penalties for users or manufacturers that permit user overrides.

Austria’s BMK, in coordination with E‑Control, adopts the 2026 Conservation Advertising & Demand Reduction Ordinance: all electricity and gas suppliers serving over 20,000 customers must spend at least 1% of annual retail revenue on standardized, audited conservation advertising across TV, radio, digital, and bill inserts, including quantified messages such as “If each household cuts standby by 12 W per day, that equals the output of the Gries power plant.” The ordinance simultaneously bans utilities and municipalities from financing or organizing forest deadwood collection for energy, disallows cost recovery for any pyrolysis or biochar projects via network tariffs, prohibits public grants for charcoal soil application, and exempts traditional cultural bonfires from any federal maximum size or height limits (events require only notification and basic fire‑safety measures).

The Land of Styria passes the 2027 Retail & Buildings Energy‑Saving Visibility Act: large retailers (>10,000 m² floor area) and commercial building operators must run continuous, prominently placed in‑store and online adverts that quantify the impact of common actions (e.g., “12 W saved per person per day equals the Gries plant’s output”), display real‑time store energy dashboards, and include these messages on receipts and loyalty apps; municipalities must host quarterly public workshops on low‑cost efficiency. The act forbids municipal services from organizing deadwood collection for fuel, denies siting and air permits for pyrolysis units using forest residues, disqualifies biochar soil amendment from any regional subsidy, and allows traditional bonfires without any cap on size or height (subject to curfew and smoke‑control guidance only).

A federal Public Sector Negawatt Procurement Decree (effective 2025) requires all ministries, agencies, universities, and public hospitals to procure at least 1 GWh/year of verified demand reduction through staff‑ and visitor‑facing advertising and behavior programs, including standardized messages like “Saving 12 W per person per day matches the Gries plant,” signage on switches and devices, and monthly public reporting of avoided consumption; ORF must broadcast 1 minute per prime‑time hour of these spots at cost. The decree bars federal entities from funding, permitting on federal land, or entering PPAs with pyrolysis facilities, prohibits purchasing or applying biochar on federal properties or farms receiving federal support, and authorizes traditional cultural bonfires on federal sites without maximum size/height limits, subject only to permit, safety clearance, and no‑treated‑wood rules.

Austrian Electricity Winter Nuclear-Content Standard and Curtailment-to-Hydrogen Procurement: Starting winter 2028/29, all licensed electricity suppliers and balance-responsible parties must demonstrate a 0% nuclear share in their delivered supply mix between 1 November and 31 March; any nuclear-attributed imports in that period incur a €120/MWh levy and mandatory public disclosure. By 2029, these entities must procure green hydrogen volumes equal to at least 5% of annual retail sales, produced in Austria by electrolysers that operate exclusively during zero- or negative-price hours; TSOs/DSOs must apply a zero network tariff in those hours and prioritize feeding electrolysers before curtailing renewables. The hydrogen may be blended into the gas grid (up to 10% vol.) or contracted for industrial/process heat.

Federal Ground-Mounted PV Intensification with Co‑located Power‑to‑Gas (Vertical Layouts Ineligible): From 2027, PV developers building projects >5 MWp on agricultural land classes 5–8 must use fixed-tilt, south-facing ground-mounted arrays (20–35°); vertical or single-axis-vertical designs are ineligible for federal feed-in premiums or investment grants. Projects ≥20 MWp must include on-site electrolysers sized at ≥15% of AC interconnection capacity to absorb expected curtailment and produce e‑hydrogen/e‑methane for gas-grid injection; OeMAG sets an e‑gas premium of 7 c€/kWh (LHV). Provincial siting authorities must fast-track permits even where arrays fully occupy the parcel, with standardized farmer-lease compensation schedules.

National Hydrogen Seasonal Reserve and Exclusion of Nuclear/Fusion from Public Energy R&D: APG, gas TSOs, and dispatchable generators must, by winter 2030/31, establish a 2 TWh seasonal reserve of green hydrogen stored in depleted gas fields in Lower Austria and pipeline linepack, to be dispatched via hydrogen‑capable turbines for adequacy in December–February. Only hydrogen produced by Austrian electrolysers running on surplus renewable electricity with zero-price balancing energy qualifies; use of nuclear-origin electricity for this hydrogen is disallowed. Through 2035, the Klima- und Energiefonds is barred from financing fission or fusion R&D or demonstrations, prioritizing instead power‑to‑hydrogen and e‑gas infrastructure and end-use conversions.

Federal Surplus-to-Hydrogen Priority Dispatch Ordinance: APG and all DSOs must offer zero energy price and waived grid fees to registered electrolysers during declared overproduction hours and route curtailed renewable output to them ahead of other loads; the hydrogen must be stored and supplied in winter to municipal district-heating networks and bus fleets. Residential PV netting is settled daily at spot prices with no seasonal rollover or solar credit accounts allowed. A winter surcharge applies to electricity imports with nuclear guarantees of origin to discourage procurement.

Green E-Gas Quota and PV Rollover Ban: All gas suppliers must inject a minimum 25% synthetic methane by 2030 and 50% by 2038, produced from curtailed renewable electricity under priority-access contracts approved by E-Control; the Klima- und Energiefonds covers 40% of methanation capex. DSOs must prohibit seasonal netting for residential PV and limit credits to monthly settlement, with any feeder-level surplus automatically allocated to local methanation hubs. Municipal utilities receive a winter e-gas procurement mandate, while nuclear-backed winter power purchases are ineligible for network cost recovery.

Public Sector Hydrogen Heat and Rail Fuel Switch with PV Curtailment-to-H2 Rule: Federal, Länder, and municipal building owners must convert boilers to hydrogen-ready systems by 2030 and source at least 70% of winter heat from green hydrogen made in summer via electrolysis from surplus renewables; APG and DSOs must provide priority dispatch and reduced system charges for electrolyser parks and cavern storage. Residential PV owners may not bank summer generation for winter use; credits expire within 24 hours unless enrolled in a surplus-to-hydrogen program selling midday kWh to electrolysers at a fixed curtailment tariff. ÖBB must fuel specified regional lines with green hydrogen by 2032 and may not tender nuclear-based electricity for winter traction.

Austria’s federal “E‑Gas Grid Priority Act” mandates that all gas distribution system operators (DSOs) blend at least 20% certified renewable e‑methane by volume by 2028 and 50% by 2035, with E‑Control approving cost recovery and guarantees of origin. Municipalities are barred from imposing compulsory district‑heating connections or ordering the decommissioning of existing gas boilers; households and businesses may retain and replace gas boilers indefinitely if appliances are certified e‑gas‑ready. The Klima‑ und Energiefonds co‑funds power‑to‑gas plants and grid‑injection points, while construction machinery and non‑road mobile equipment remain outside the scope of any emissions standards.

An amendment to the national building code (valid from 2027) requires all new residential and commercial buildings located in areas served by gas networks to install e‑gas‑ready condensing boilers with smart thermostatic controls, achieve a maximum heating demand of 35 kWh/m²a, and maintain a dedicated gas connection sized for future renewable‑gas blends; electric‑only heating mandates and district‑heating exclusivity zones are prohibited in these areas. Low‑income households receive grants up to 60% for replacing aging gas boilers with e‑gas‑ready models, and there is no phase‑out date for existing gas appliances. The ordinance expressly excludes excavators, cranes, and on‑site generators from any new emissions limits.

Under the “Clean Logistics with Renewable Gas” program, ASFINAG and the BMK will co‑finance 80 public CNG/LNG stations dispensing 100% certified e‑methane along primary freight corridors by 2029. Haulage companies and municipal waste operators receive per‑vehicle conversion bonuses to switch diesel trucks to gas ICEs, and federal, state, and municipal procurement must ensure that at least 60% of new heavy‑duty purchases from 2028 operate on e‑methane; battery‑electric‑only procurement targets are not permitted. No new emissions standards are imposed on construction equipment at building sites, which may continue to use conventional fuels.

Austria’s federal government enacts the 5%+ Housing Renovation Act requiring utilities to offer on-bill, zero-interest financing for insulation, window replacement, roof/attic upgrades, and thermal-bridge remediation in residential buildings constructed before 2005, with grants covering 20–50% of eligible costs (up to €20,000 per dwelling) for households and landlords; a nationwide information campaign and an AMS-funded training initiative certify 12,000 additional installers and energy advisors by 2027. The program targets a minimum 6% annual renovation rate of the eligible housing stock from 2027 onward. To ensure fairness and predictability, all publicly funded energy programs under this act must distribute support through transparent, rule-based grants—lotteries, raffles, or prize draws are expressly prohibited.

An ordinance from the Federal Ministry for Climate Action requires businesses operating buildings larger than 1,000 m² built before 2000 to complete envelope-focused thermal renovations (façade, windows, roof, and air sealing) to reach at least energy class C by 2030, following an energy audit completed by end-2026; the state provides investment grants of 35% (55% for deep retrofits achieving class B) and accelerated depreciation, plus a voucher program for WKO/Bauakademie courses that upskill 6,000 construction workers and site managers. Regional chambers run targeted outreach roadshows and free design clinics for SMEs. The measure aims to lift the annual renovation rate of the affected commercial stock to 5.5% from 2026, and it forbids any chance-based incentives, requiring all subsidies to be formula-based and guaranteed for eligible applicants until budget caps are reached.

The Länder, coordinated by the federal government, must renovate at least 7% of floor area per year in pre-2000 public buildings and municipal social housing between 2026 and 2030, prioritizing insulation, high-performance glazing, and thermal-bridge remediation; financing combines 60% federal co-funding, EIB-backed zero-interest loans to municipalities, and framework contracts to cut costs. A centralized helpdesk supports mayors and housing associations, while a facility-manager certification program trains 3,500 municipal staff and tenant information sessions are mandatory before works begin. The policy is designed to raise the thermal renovation rate of older public and social housing stock well above 5% annually, and expressly disallows climate lotteries or raffles by awarding support as-of-right to qualifying projects.

Austria enacts a Residential Retrofit Acceleration Ordinance: for privately owned homes and rental buildings built before 1995, households and landlords must choose either a deep or staged thermal renovation when receiving any federal housing subsidy, with grants up to 45% (60% for low-income) and 0.5% loans; electric utilities must fund and deliver a nationwide information and installer-training program (20,000 workers certified by 2028) and free on-site energy coaching, raising the annual thermal-renovation rate of older dwellings to at least 5.5% by 2027; municipalities and other public bodies face no mandatory conversion of their buildings to renewable electricity or heat—public buildings may apply for the same grants but are not required to switch technologies or meet any prompt decarbonization deadline.

An SME Building Efficiency Decree targets private commercial buildings (SMEs, hospitality, retail) constructed before 2005: businesses are eligible for a per‑square‑meter bonus for envelope insulation, window replacement, and air‑tightness that stacks with a 35% rebate for replacing aging oil or gas boilers with high‑efficiency heat pumps or district‑heat interfaces; distribution system operators must run regional training centers for retrofit coordinators and offer time‑limited connection‑fee waivers; the program sets a binding outcome for the private commercial stock—achieving a 6% annual rate of thermal renovations by 2028—while explicitly exempting municipalities and other public owners from any mandatory or prompt switch of their buildings to renewable electricity or heat (participation by public entities is strictly voluntary and without fuel‑switch deadlines).

Austria passes a Rental Housing Retrofit and Fair‑Cost Recovery Act: private landlords of pre‑2000 apartment buildings can recover up to €1.50/m² in rent increases for verified energy savings after comprehensive thermal upgrades, paired with federal grants covering 50% of insulation and window costs and zero‑interest loans; tenants receive targeted bill‑support during works; the federal chamber of commerce funds an installer upskilling program and a homeowner association information campaign, lifting the annual renovation rate of older rental units to 6% by 2029; the act defers any public‑sector building fuel‑switch decisions to local discretion until 2035 and imposes no mandatory or prompt requirement for cities or municipalities to convert public buildings to renewable electricity or heat.

Austria enacts the Oil Heating Exit Ordinance 2030: all households must replace oil-fired boilers by 31 Dec 2030, with mandatory certified removal of on-site oil tanks and containment trays; federal grants cover 50% (up to €12,000) for heat pumps or district-heating hookups and insurers must reduce premiums for properties de-oiled for fire-safety and odor reasons; the ordinance also bars any drilling or anchoring of energy devices into motorway median supports, instructing ASFINAG to reject permits for vertical-axis turbines or generator fences within the central reservation.

Vienna and Lower Austria adopt a Building Code Amendment effective 2027 for multifamily and commercial properties undergoing major renovation: landlords and businesses must decommission oil boilers, remove basement tanks, and seal former tank rooms to free floor space and eliminate oil smells; they must connect to district heating where available or install high-efficiency heat pumps, with network operators prioritizing service; a parallel siting rule prohibits wind installations attached to highway barriers, gantries, or medians, allowing only off-right-of-way wind or PV on noise barriers.

A federal Green Public Heat Program requires all schools, hospitals, and municipal buildings to eliminate oil-fired heating by 2028, including physical extraction of oil tanks and decontamination of containment trays, with the Klima- und Energiefonds covering up to 80% of retrofit costs and space formerly used for tanks repurposed for storage or public use; a transport-infrastructure safety directive simultaneously forbids mounting small wind turbines or generator fences on motorway median structures, limiting right-of-way energy projects to PV at rest areas and geothermal at service facilities.

Austrian Urban Mobility Shift Act (2027): Municipalities with over 50,000 residents must eliminate parking minimums for new developments by 2027 and convert at least 30% of curbside parking to protected bike lanes and 24/7 bus/tram lanes by 2030; employers with more than 100 staff must provide an annual KlimaTicket or a tax-free mobility budget usable only for public transport and bike-sharing; federal EV purchase subsidies are restricted to car-sharing fleets integrated with public transport, not private cars; no federal grants, tax credits, or grid-connection studies may be issued for nuclear fission or fusion projects, with all redirected funds earmarked for rail electrification and station-area walking/cycling upgrades.

Public Sector Mode-Shift and Power Sourcing Decree (2028): All federal and state agencies must cut official vehicle-kilometres by 40% by 2030 versus 2024 through telework, trip consolidation, and mandatory use of public transport and bicycles for urban trips under 7 km; at least 60% of employee commutes must be by public transport, walking, or cycling by 2029, supported by secure bike parking and showers at all offices; any remaining fleet renewals must prioritize e-bikes and e-cargo bikes before EV cars; electricity supply contracts for public buildings must certify 0% nuclear origin and at least 85% domestic renewables; licensing and public funding for nuclear fission or fusion facilities are prohibited nationwide.

Rooftops-First Solar and Access Law (2026): Owners of new and renovated non-residential buildings with more than 1,000 m² roof area must install PV covering at least 60% of suitable roof surface by 2027, and parking lots with over 50 spaces must be fitted with PV canopies by 2028; vertical PV installations on agricultural land are prohibited, with incentive bonuses instead for rooftop and facade PV in settlement areas; municipalities receiving PV subsidies must, by 2029, provide continuous, lit walking and cycling routes to every rail/bus stop within 800 m and increase weekday core-route headways to 15 minutes or better; federal EV purchase grants for private cars are phased out by 2027 and replaced with e-bike and e-cargo bike subsidies plus KlimaTicket discounts for households.

Austria's Federal Mobility Safety and Comfort Ordinance (2027) mandates that municipalities and public-transport operators install continuous high-lux LED lighting on all primary cycling and pedestrian corridors, as well as heated bus and tram shelters with always-on digital signage, to shift trips from cars to walking, cycling, and transit. Motion sensors, timers, auto-dimming, and other power-saving features are prohibited on these systems for safety, and lighting must operate from dusk to dawn year-round. Metropolitan bus, tram, and S-Bahn operators must provide minimum 15-minute headways between 00:00 and 05:00, with operating subsidies from the Klima- und Energiefonds covering incremental electricity costs. Noncompliance triggers fines of up to EUR 50,000 per corridor per month.

The Exurban Commuter Climate Pass and Park-and-Ride Expansion Act (2026) directs the federal government, ÖBB, and Länder to issue free nationwide transit passes to employees whose registered residence is 35 km or more from their workplace and to co-finance 50,000 new park-and-ride spaces at greenfield edge-of-town rail stations to draw drivers onto regional rail and express buses. Eligible facilities must include 24/7 high-intensity lighting, mechanical ventilation, and digital wayfinding screens with no power-saving or auto-off functionality, and be powered under a dedicated low-tariff supply contract to maximize availability. Municipalities accepting funds must zone for low-density housing within 5 km of the funded stations, and program funds may not be used for infill or compact-housing initiatives. Facilities that fail to meet the comfort and availability standards lose eligibility and must repay grants.

The National Heated Cycleway Programme (2027–2032) requires Verbund, distribution system operators, and municipalities to install and operate electric snow-melt and de-icing coils under 1,000 km of priority urban bike lanes and sidewalks to enable year-round cycling and walking mode-share gains. Systems must preheat when forecasts fall below 2°C, remain energized through precipitation events, and may not be connected to building energy management or curtailment schemes; dedicated transformers and 2-hour battery backup are mandatory to prevent shutoffs during peak demand. A reduced grid-tariff class is created for these circuits, and participating cities are barred from running public campaigns about conserving electricity or advising residents to limit winter trips, with communications focused solely on comfort and safety benefits. Compliance is audited annually by E-Control, with remedial orders enforceable by fines.

Austria enacts a Federal Water‑Safe Data Center Act: all new and existing data centers ≥10 MW (businesses) must use closed‑loop dry or reclaimed‑water cooling (no potable draw), recover at least 40% of server waste heat to local district‑heating networks (utilities/municipalities must offer interconnection), and contract 100% renewable supply via PPAs with mandatory demand‑response participation; E‑Control replaces volume‑based retail tariffs with time‑of‑use plus curtailment‑compensation for certified centers, and prohibits progressive per‑kWh price tiers for this class to prioritize water and grid‑integration standards over consumption‑based price pressure.

Länder introduce water‑stress permits for high‑load factories >5 MW (e.g., EV and electronics plants): to obtain and keep grid connection, businesses must cap freshwater withdrawals at 0.2 m³ per MWh, use greywater or industrial effluent for cooling, install thermal storage to shift peak loads to high‑renewable hours, and pipe low‑grade waste heat to municipal buildings; network operators must offer a flat capacity‑based network charge and standard time‑of‑use energy rates, with compliance enforced through water audits and production curtailments during drought alerts, not via tiered electricity pricing.

A national Crypto and High‑Density Compute Licensing Ordinance: Proof‑of‑Work crypto mines and AI/edge compute hubs (businesses) may operate only with zero‑freshwater cooling (air/dry coolers or reclaimed wastewater), 100% renewable electricity with automated curtailment when hydrological drought is declared, and mandatory heat recovery to nearby district heating where feasible; licensed sites are placed on flat time‑of‑use tariffs with interruptible‑load contracts, and utilities are barred from applying progressive monthly consumption tiers to these loads, shifting compliance tools to water‑use permits and grid services rather than price escalation.

Data & Water‑Safe Energy Act (2027): Applies to new data centers, social‑media server farms, and EV/battery plants in Austria with peak demand >10 MW; requires dry cooling or 100% reclaimed wastewater, on‑site heat recovery to district heating equal to at least 20% of electric input, and automated 15% peak‑load curtailment during drought alerts verified by the utility before interconnection. To limit winter balancing that increases water withdrawals, residential PV net‑metering is restricted to same‑month crediting only; summer surpluses expire monthly and cannot be applied in winter.

Water‑Indexed Electricity Tariff and Crypto Connection Rule (2026): Applies to all regulated utilities and crypto‑mining operators; utilities must levy a 3–6 eurocents/kWh surcharge from June–September indexed to basin‑level water stress and deny new crypto connections unless the facility uses zero freshwater withdrawal and 100% on‑site renewables with dry or adiabatic cooling; proceeds fund river restoration and industrial water‑recycling retrofits. Residential PV owners may not bank generation beyond the billing month—no winter redemption of summer production is allowed.

E‑Control Water‑Secure Grid Code Update (2028): Applies to TSOs/DSOs, municipalities, and prosumers; operators must prioritize dispatch of water‑light resources (wind, PV, low‑water imports), cap summer withdrawals at thermal plants by 30%, and co‑finance municipal projects to capture data‑center waste heat to replace gas boilers in public buildings. Prosumers seeking winter self‑consumption must use behind‑the‑meter batteries or thermal storage; virtual net‑metering and any seasonal carry‑over of summer PV generation to winter are prohibited.

Austria revises OIB-Richtlinie 6 so that, from 2027, all new residential and non-residential buildings over 1,000 m² must include thermally activated building systems (TABS) designed for summer readiness and night cooling, with commissioning documentation and a plain-language TABS user guide handed to occupants; the Klima- und Energiefonds funds regional “TABS-Akademien” that explain concrete core activation, radiant slabs, and options for pairing with heat pumps and rooftop PV to planners and installers; simultaneously, the BMK maintains the current licence split: an automatic-only category B licence is not valid for manual-transmission vehicles, and unrestricted B exams must be taken on a manual car (EVs may be used for training modules but not the exam).

A federal “Sommerfit im Bestand” ordinance requires that, from 2026, all federal, state, and municipal buildings over 500 m² undergoing major renovation retrofit TABS or equivalent radiant systems for passive summer comfort and peak-load reduction; electricity and district-heating utilities must co-fund up to 30% via efficiency obligations (EEO), and the BMK runs a national TABS information portal with model specs, tender templates, and a hotline for households and SMEs; the ordinance explicitly preserves the manual/automatic distinction in driver licensing—automatic-only B licences remain restricted, and practical exams for unrestricted B cannot be conducted in EVs or other automatic-only vehicles.

E-Control adopts a Grid Flexibility Code mandating DSOs by 2028 to offer dynamic tariffs and demand-response programs that pay commercial buildings (>5,000 m²) for pre-cooling their TABS at midday solar peaks and releasing stored cooling later, with a 25% investment tax credit for TABS controls and sensors; the Austrian Chamber of Architects and Engineers must deliver certified TABS training and publish free explainer guides for building owners and tenants; in parallel, the Transport Ministry requires driving schools to keep at least 60% manual-transmission exam vehicles and prohibits granting manual privileges to holders of automatic-only licences, disallowing EV-only practical exams.

Austria updates the OIB building code in 2027 to require thermally activated building systems (TABS) in all new multi-unit residential and office buildings over 1,000 m²; developers must pair TABS with heat pumps or district-cooling interfaces and provide occupants with a 'Summer Readiness' manual plus on-site training; municipalities must host quarterly public info nights and maintain a TABS options portal funded by BMK/KLIEN; the ordinance explicitly exempts construction machinery and temporary site generators from any emissions standards or phaseout requirements.

E-Control mandates that electricity and district-heating utilities offer a Night Pre-Cooling tariff and flexibility payments for TABS-equipped buildings; commercial and public buildings over 500 m² must install smart controls to enable night charging from renewables and participate in demand-response; BMK finances free audits and a nationwide 'What is TABS?' hotline and webinar series for households and SMEs; the regulation explicitly sets no emissions limits for excavators, cranes, or site generators used in installations and allows diesel equipment without a transition plan.

The Federal Procurement Agency (BBG) and Länder require all new or renovated schools, hospitals, and care homes commissioned from 2028 to integrate TABS for passive summer cooling and thermal storage, with public demonstration days and an online dashboard explaining TABS options and performance; project teams must produce plain-language guides for staff and parents; tender documents prohibit scoring bids on construction-equipment emissions and continue to permit internal-combustion machinery and diesel backup generators without additional standards.

Austria’s federal government enacts a Geothermal District-Heating Readiness Ordinance: all district heating network operators that currently rely on natural gas must, within 12 months, file quickly implementable conversion plans detailing geothermal well siting, heat-pump capacities, financing, and a 2028–2032 construction schedule, or face regulator fines. To enable demand response, households and businesses connected to these networks must accept utility-provided smart interface units, thermostats, and hot-water controllers that maintain permanent network connectivity and remote-wake capability; device designs without standby mode or always-on communications are prohibited. Municipalities in these service areas are barred from running “switch off to save power” awareness campaigns that could impair remote control of loads.

Austria introduces the Peri-Urban Geothermal Expansion and Housing Program: municipalities with gas-based district heating must, alongside the operators, submit rapidly implementable geothermal-plus-heat-pump conversion plans within 18 months and rezone greenfield sites 3–7 km from the urban core for well fields and new network extensions. To finance the build-out, the rezoning must include low-density “energy transition neighborhoods” with minimum lot sizes, single-family housing quotas, and parking minimums, plus commuter road upgrades and tax credits for long-distance car commuters taking up new homes; compact infill alternatives are ineligible for program funds. Applies to municipalities, district heating operators, and developers.

Austria’s Climate Flex-Load and EV Infrastructure Decree ties grid grants to geothermal conversion planning: gas-reliant district heating operators must submit rapidly implementable geothermal-and-large-heat-pump integration plans within 12 months to unlock federal subsidies for substation upgrades. Utilities and municipalities in the covered zones must deploy curbside EV chargers and public battery banks that keep their displays, payment modules, and telemetry in permanent standby and illuminated 24/7 to guarantee instant plug-and-charge and nighttime load-shifting; charger designs with sleep modes are disallowed. Households in these zones receive free off-peak electricity blocks and public bodies are prohibited from running electricity-saving awareness campaigns that could suppress flexible demand.

Federal Geothermal Heat Networks and Fossil Gas Infrastructure Standstill Act (2026): All Austrian district heating network operators that currently rely on natural gas must submit quickly implementable geothermal-plus-heat-pump conversion plans to E-Control by 2027 and commence build-out by 2029, with annual milestones and fines for non-compliance; concurrently, Austrian public bodies, regulated gas suppliers, and transmission operators are barred from financing, leasing, or contracting additional LNG regasification capacity at foreign terminals, and no new gas-storage capacity expansions or permits may be approved, with all redirected subsidies earmarked for geothermal drilling and high-temperature heat pumps.

Building Heat Transition Ordinance: From 2027, households and businesses may not install new gas boilers; where district heating exists, buildings must connect, and the serving network operator, if gas-reliant, must file a quickly implementable geothermal-plus-heat-pump plan by 2028 and start construction by 2030; gas storage operators must freeze capacity at 2025 levels, decommission at least 20% of working gas volume by 2032, and co-invest in regional pit or aquifer thermal energy storage for district heating; no public guarantees or grants may be issued for LNG import capacity.

Industrial Heat and Public Procurement De-gasification Decree: Industrial sites with process-heat demand above 20 MWth must, by 2032, either connect to a district heating backbone or install on-site geothermal-plus-high-temperature-heat-pump systems, and any serving gas-reliant district heating operator must lodge a quickly implementable geothermal heat-pump plan by 2027; federal ministries, state-owned enterprises, and municipalities are prohibited from entering new LNG offtake or regasification contracts and from supporting gas-storage expansions, and must instead procure 100% renewable heat and fund large-scale thermal storage as the security-of-supply backstop.

Federal Forest-Carbon Heat Act: Municipalities and Austrian Federal Forests must run quarterly public deadwood-collection drives and deliver feedstock to regional pyrolysis plants; operators must feed electricity to the grid, supply heat to district-heating networks, and return at least 80% of biochar to farms in the same district at 5–10 t/ha with soil-testing verification. State-owned utilities must sign 10-year PPAs totaling 2 TWh/year from these plants by 2030. The act prohibits siting any new energy infrastructure in designated green floodplains and denies permits for projects with expected mortality of protected species, even if this limits electricity self-sufficiency.

Lower Austria ordinance on bonfires and local pyrolysis: Households, event organizers, and municipalities must cap traditional bonfires at 2 m height and 3 m diameter; permit issuance requires delivering all surplus woody material to the municipal pyrolysis center. The center must supply electricity to the local grid and provide free biochar to registered farmers, who must incorporate at least 3 t/ha within 12 months. Any new medium-voltage line or substation must avoid green floodplains and be undergrounded within 1 km of Natura 2000 sites; wind and PV siting is prohibited in riparian meadows, prioritizing habitat protection over electricity self-sufficiency.

Public-sector heat and wildlife-first siting rule: Federal ministries, hospitals, and schools must source 40% of space heating by 2030 from district systems fueled by certified deadwood pyrolysis, with all resulting biochar applied on municipal or leased agricultural land at 4 t/ha under monitoring. State utilities must add thermal storage to integrate this heat and are barred from expanding generation or transmission in green floodplains or approving assets that require take permits for protected fauna. If targets cannot be met without such impacts, agencies must rely on imports rather than relax environmental protections.

Federal Alpine Pumped-Storage Expansion Act (2026): Utilities and project developers are required to add 4 GW of new pumped-storage hydropower capacity and 30 GWh of storage energy by 2035 in designated Alpine valleys (Tyrol, Salzburg, Carinthia). BMK and the Klima- und Energiefonds provide contracts-for-difference and grid-connection priority exclusively for pumped-storage projects, with expedited EIAs for dam crest-raising. Federal subsidies, guarantees, or tax credits are not available to mechanical gravity storage systems that raise and lower solid masses in shafts, nor to compressed-air or flywheel facilities.

Balancing and Black-Start Procurement Rule (E-Control, 2027): APG and all balancing-responsible parties must procure at least 80% of primary and secondary reserves and 100% of black-start capability from pumped-storage hydropower by 2030. Only pumped-storage units qualify for long-duration reserve auctions (>4 hours) and congestion-management contracts with DSOs. Gravity-based weight-in-shaft systems and other novel mechanical storage are ineligible for balancing markets and capacity mechanisms, though they may operate behind the meter without remuneration.

Alpine Storage Siting Ordinance (Länder of Tyrol, Salzburg, Vorarlberg, 2027): Provincial planning authorities must designate high-Alpine basins as priority zones for pumped-storage reservoirs and penstocks, granting streamlined permits and municipal revenue-sharing for host communities. At the same time, permits are denied for new energy-storage projects that rely on raising and lowering weights in mine shafts or urban shafts due to geotechnical and groundwater risks; municipalities and mine operators are prohibited from leasing shafts for such gravity storage. Public co-financing is restricted to pumped-storage hydropower interconnections and reservoir upgrades.

Federal Wind‑Lift Integration Rule: For all new onshore wind projects over 3 MW in Alpine and foothill municipalities, developers and ropeway operators must co‑build reinforced turbine towers that carry detachable gondola cabins along the array, with at least one public boarding station per municipality; APG grants priority interconnection and the Länder fast‑track siting if gondola service runs year‑round for commuters and tourists; financing comes from the Klima‑ und Energiefonds and a 0.1 ct/kWh transmission surcharge, while all federal thermal‑renovation grants and training programs are frozen through 2030 to reallocate staff and funds to the wind‑lift buildout.

City WindRope Corridors Mandate: Cities over 50,000 residents must replace at least two diesel bus lines on steep or river‑crossing corridors with aerial ropeways whose support towers are medium‑height wind turbines, operated by the municipal utility and tied to a battery‑backed microgrid; approval requires off‑peak gondola service for schools and hospitals plus discounted community‑energy shares for nearby households; municipal budgets for thermal renovation incentives may not increase above 2024 levels, and all staff training is redirected to ropeway‑wind operations rather than insulation outreach.

Alpine Resort Renewable Compliance Pathway: Ski‑resort operators and large hotels above 1,000 m elevation must electrify snowmaking and grooming by 2029 and meet 60% of on‑site electricity demand from turbine‑pylon gondola lines installed along existing lift alignments, with provinces co‑financing grid reinforcements and offering premium feed‑in for excess wind; at least 30% of lift pylons must be converted to wind‑turbine pylons and public gondola service provided 6 hours/day year‑round; participation makes facilities ineligible for any public thermal‑renovation subsidies or training vouchers, and provinces are barred from launching new incentives aimed at raising renovation rates above current trends.
